The above results are obtained from a given batch of images using data parallelism in the GPU.

The scope of this library is to not provide explicitly optimized code for vision, but we want to show an experiment comparing the performance of our library with respect to other existing vision libraries e.g. OpenCV [9], PIL, skimage [56] and scipy [42], see figure 2.

abstract: This work presents Kornia – an open source computer vision library which consists of a set of differentiable routines and modules to solve generic computer vision problems. The package uses PyTorch as its main backend both for efficiency and to take advantage of the reverse-mode auto-differentiation to define and compute the gradient of complex functions. Inspired by OpenCV, Kornia is composed of a set of modules containing operators that can be inserted inside neural networks to train models to perform image transformations, camera calibration, epipolar geometry, and low level image processing techniques, such as filtering and edge detection that operate directly on high dimensional tensor representations. Examples of classical vision problems implemented using our framework are provided including a benchmark comparing to existing vision libraries.

sections.body: The paper introduces Kornia, an open source computer vision library built on PyTorch. It notes that torchvision lacks standard vision algorithms that run directly on GPUs with native tensors. Table 1 compares libraries on CPU, GPU, batch processing, differentiability, distribution and multi-dimensional arrays. It marks Kornia and tensorflow.image as the only frameworks that mostly implement their functions on GPU, with batched data, differentiably and with distribution. Figure 1 shows low-level processing results. The demos cover image registration, depth estimation and local feature detection.
sections.heading: Introduction
sections.headline: Kornia is presented as a PyTorch computer vision library that runs classical image operations on GPUs as differentiable modules.

sections.body: The review covers traditional libraries such as OpenCV, VLFeat, the MATLAB Computer Vision Toolbox and scikit-image, which mostly target CPUs. It states that most deep learning frameworks still use standard vision libraries such as OpenCV or PIL for CPU pre- and post-processing. Table 1 shows tensorflow.image as the closest alternative. The authors therefore propose a PyTorch-based library offering differentiability, batched CPU and GPU operation, distributed computing and production readiness.
sections.heading: Related work
sections.headline: Prior vision libraries are mostly CPU-based, and deep learning frameworks rely on them for pre- and post-processing.

sections.body: Kornia exposes high-level interfaces to vision algorithms that act directly on tensors. Operators can be placed inside neural networks and trained by backpropagation through reverse-mode auto-differentiation. Inputs are batches of N-channel tensors, and the same API runs on CPU or GPU. Distributed support covers multi-process parallelism across computation nodes. Production use relies on PyTorch tracing to TorchScript. The modules are `kornia.color`, `kornia.features`, `kornia.filters`, `kornia.geometry`, `kornia.losses` and `kornia.contrib`, where contrib holds experimental operators.
sections.heading: Kornia: Computer Vision for PyTorch.
sections.headline: Kornia is organized into PyTorch-based submodules whose operators are differentiable, batched, device-agnostic and usable across distributed systems.

sections.body: Batch processing: Sobel edges are computed 500 times on 256x256 RGB batches of varying size, and the median elapsed time is reported. Kornia performs similarly to other libraries on small batches. On large batches its CPU path is the slowest, while its GPU path gives the best timing. Registration: a homography is optimized by Adam with learning rate 1e-3 for 200 iterations at each pyramid scale. Depth: 3 calibrated 320x240 views are processed with SGD and momentum at 7 scales, using SceneNet RGB-D data, and results are described as partial. Adversarial: perturbations make a non-matching pair yield homography-consistent matches using the Hessian detector, SIFT descriptors, the top-2500 keypoints and Adam at learning rate 0.003. The authors state the perturbations are not quite imperceptible.
sections.heading: Use cases
sections.headline: Four use cases test the library on Sobel timing, homography registration, depth estimation and adversarial matching.

sections.body: The conclusion restates that Kornia implements traditional vision algorithms in a differentiable way and uses hardware acceleration. Image registration by homography, depth estimation and local feature matching are described as solvable with performance similar to existing libraries. The authors expect classical libraries to serve as network layers and as pre- and post-processing components. At submission, the project had 660 github stars and 60 forks.
sections.heading: Conclusions
sections.headline: Classical vision tasks are reported to solve easily in PyTorch with performance similar to existing libraries.
